body.text: Russia's Vladimir Putin in a press conference following his visit to China (Kremlin)
What does Putin really mean by dangling a “compromise” over Ukraine?
Russia’s new openness to European involvement in talks looks more like opportunism than concession.

Negotiations rarely begin when the parties involved are already close to agreement. But through successive rounds of talks, the parties gradually move closer together and may become willing to make concessions as circumstances change. There have been no meaningful negotiations about ending Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, more a series of pantomime meetings while the Kremlin has sought to press for advantage on the battlefield. Yet Putin’s reference to “compromise” might be the beginning of something.
Nothing out of the Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral added to the pressure on Russia to end this war, but it might signal that diplomacy is at least becoming a serious part of the conversation.

Russia’s negotiating position is hardline, but “compromise” might be indicated by the recent change in Russia's position regarding European participation in peace negotiations – something Moscow had previously resisted. Or maybe that is itself a ploy for more time, the Kremlin knowing that major European states including Germany and France see the march of right-wing political parties, many of which oppose continued spending on the war in Ukraine. Electoral success by Germany’s Alternative for Germany (AfD) or France’s National Rally with Marine Le Pen as its presidential candidate could reverse support of Ukraine among two of its biggest donors.

This evolving European political context, coupled with the pressure from the United States, might also shape how Ukraine makes decisions on its concessions and demands for the cessation of hostilities. Putin’s “compromise” suddenly appears less accommodating.

There are many expert analyses suggesting that Russia has no genuine interest in peacemaking because it remains committed to continuing the war and seeks to gain further territory in Ukraine and potentially has a broader goal of waging war with Europe. Nothing out of the Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral added to the pressure on Russia to end this war, but it might signal that diplomacy is at least becoming a serious part of the conversation.
